title: I Already Know That
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Leaders who reflexively tell team members 'I already know that' create a self-sealing information failure. The response signals that the team member's input is unwelcome, which causes them to pre-filter what they share—and the information most likely to be filtered is precisely the kind that is awkward, uncertain, or only partially formed: exactly what matters most. Over time, the leader accumulates updates without accumulating genuine intelligence, growing increasingly isolated from early warning signs while believing they are well-informed. The antidote is deliberate curiosity: replacing dismissal with expansion ('Tell me more,' 'What's changed?') and periodically asking whether the information environment has quietly narrowed. The leader who stays approachable rather than reflexively certain is the one most likely to hear the one detail that changes everything.
points: Saying 'I already know that' teaches team members to pre-filter information, causing the leader to learn less about the things that matter most.
The information most likely to get filtered out is exactly what leaders most need: the awkward, uncertain, or only-partially-formed early signal.
Replacing 'I already know that' with 'Tell me more' or 'What's changed?' expands the information environment rather than constricting it.
Good leaders audit their information environment periodically—asking whether people have simply stopped bothering to tell them things.
The habit of reflexive certainty ('I already know that') belongs on the same list as 'That won't work,' 'I'll just do it myself,' and 'Why didn't you say something sooner?'
quotes: Whenever a leader tells a team member, “I already know that,” they are sending an unintended message that the team member should filter or censor the information they share.
Once a team member senses that their updates are redundant or unwanted, they begin pre-filtering everything before it reaches the leader.
People tend to hold back precisely the things that feel awkward, uncertain, or only partially formed.
The leader who signals impatience with “already known” information teaches their team to withhold exactly the kind of information that matters most.
Good leaders periodically ask themselves whether the information environment around them has quietly narrowed — whether people have simply stopped bothering to tell them things.
The leader who stays genuinely curious and approachable, rather than reflexively certain, is the one most likely to hear the one detail that changes everything.
